Morrow
MOR-ō
n. (the following day; in the Authorized Version chiefly rendering Hebrew mochorāth and Greek aurion)
From Middle English morwe, from Old English morgen, morning — the same word that gives morning, narrowed to mean the morning next following, and so the next day. The Authorized Version prints it as two words in the idiom to morrow, which is simply on the morrow. The Hebrew mochorāth likewise derives from a root meaning after or behind: the morrow is what comes behind today, and what a man does not yet possess.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The morrow is Scripture's standing name for the future that belongs to God and not to us. Doctrinally it is the point at which the doctrine of providence meets the ordinary conduct of a life, and Scripture presses it from two sides. Against anxiety, the Lord commands, “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself” (Mat 6:34) — not that the believer should be improvident, for the ant provideth her meat in the summer, but that he should not carry tomorrow's burden with today's strength, since grace is issued daily like manna and will not be hoarded. Against presumption, James asks what our life is and answers that it is a vapour, appearing for a little time and vanishing away, so that to speak of tomorrow's business without if the Lord will is not planning but boasting (Jas 4:14). Solomon says the same in a proverb: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Pro 27:1). The rich fool is the parable of the sin — he had many goods laid up for many years, and the years were not his to lay up (Luk 12:20). The two commands hold together perfectly. Because the morrow is God's, I need not fear it; and because the morrow is God's, I may not presume upon it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The next following day; in Scripture the emblem of the future which belongs to God alone, forbidden as an object of anxious care and equally forbidden as a ground of boasting, since no man knows what a day may bring forth.

expand to see more

MORROW, n. The day next after the present. To morrow, that is, on the morrow; the following day.

2. In Scripture, the morrow is used for the near and uncertain future. Boast not thyself of to morrow, for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. Prov. 27.

3. The word is from the Saxon morgen, morning; the morrow is properly the next morning, and thence the next day. Good morrow, a salutation, is a wish of a good morning.

4. On the morrow; a frequent phrase of narration, marking the next stage of an action. On the morrow, when they were come from Bethany. Mark 11.

5. To take no thought for the morrow is not to forbid forecast and industry, which the Scripture elsewhere commends, but to forbid distrustful and anxious care for what is not yet given.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:34 — "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."

James 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Proverbs 27:1 — "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth."

Luke 12:20 — "But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?"

Modern Corruption

The command not to take thought for the morrow is read as a licence for improvidence on one side and dismissed as impractical sentiment on the other, while the presumption James actually condemns — planning the future as though it were owned — is celebrated as vision.

expand to see more

Mat 6:34 suffers two opposite misreadings. Some take it to forbid all forecast, saving, insurance, and provision, which sets the Lord against Solomon, who sends the sluggard to the ant, and against Paul, who says a man that provideth not for his own has denied the faith. The Authorized Version's take no thought meant in 1611 what we should now call be not anxious; the sin forbidden is distrustful care, not prudence. Others, seeing the excess of the first reading, quietly set the verse aside as unworkable in a world of mortgages and pensions. Both miss the promise the command rests on: your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things. Provision is a duty; anxiety is unbelief about a Father who has already undertaken.

The presumption side of the doctrine is scarcely resisted at all, because our age has made it a virtue. To speak confidently of what one will build in five years, without reference to whether one will be alive to build it, is called ambition and taught as a discipline. James calls it rejoicing in one's boastings, and adds that all such rejoicing is evil. The correction he gives is not paralysis but a phrase: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. It costs nothing to say and it reorders everything, because it confesses in ordinary speech that the morrow is not a possession but a gift not yet given.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mochorāth names the next day from a root meaning after. Greek aurion is the ordinary word for tomorrow, and the New Testament's decisive uses of it are all warnings — against anxiety, against boasting, and against the delay of repentance.

expand to see more

Hebrew māchār (H4279) — to morrow, in time to come; from a root meaning to be after or behind. Used in Exo 8:10, “Be it according to thy word,” where Pharaoh chooses to morrow over today.

Hebrew mochorāth (H4283) — the morrow, the day following; the narrative form, as in the morrow after the passover (Jos 5:11).

Greek aurion (G839) — to morrow, the next day; the word of Mat 6:34 and Jas 4:13, and of the good Samaritan's provision on the morrow (Luk 10:35).

Greek epaurion (G1887) — on the morrow; the narrative connective that carries the Gospel of John through its opening week (Joh 1:29, 35, 43).

Greek atmis (G822) — a vapour, a mist; the figure James sets against the morrow — a life that appeareth for a little time and then vanisheth away.

Usage

"As plain narrative sequence: on the morrow, when they were come from Bethany (Mar 11:12); the morrow after the passover (Jos 5:11)."

"As the object of forbidden anxiety: take therefore no thought for the morrow (Mat 6:34), where the Lord grounds the command on the Father's knowledge of our need."

"As the object of forbidden presumption: boast not thyself of to morrow (Pro 27:1); ye know not what shall be on the morrow (Jas 4:14); Pharaoh's fatal choice of to morrow for deliverance (Exo 8:10)."
